ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Circles with centers $ O$ and $ P$ have radii 2 and 4, respectively, and are externally tangent. Points $ A$ and $ B$ are on the circle centered at $ O$, and points $ C$ and $ D$ are on the circle centered at $ P$, such that $ \overline{AD}$ and $ \overline{BC}$ are common external tangents to the circles. What is the area of hexagon $ AOBCPD$?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a small circle with center O and radius 2, and on the right side is a large circle with center P and radius 4; the two circles are externally tangent, and the line of centers OP is horizontal. A and B are on the small circle, and D and C are on the large circle; AD is the upper common external tangent, and BC is the lower common external tangent. In the figure, OA, OB, PD, and PC are respectively the radii to the points of tangency. Reasoning: Use segment OP to divide hexagon AOBCPD into two congruent trapezoids above and below: AOPD and OBCP. Because the two circles are externally tangent, OP is equal to the sum of the two radii, namely OP = 2 + 4 = 6. For the upper common tangent AD, radii OA and PD are both perpendicular to tangent AD, so OA ∥ PD, and OA = 2, PD = 4. In the right triangle corresponding to the external common tangent, the center distance OP = 6 is the hypotenuse, and the difference of the two radii 4 - 2 = 2 is one right-angle side, so the length of tangent segment AD is sqrt(6^2 - 2^2) = sqrt(36 - 4) = sqrt(32) = 4sqrt(2). Therefore the area of trapezoid AOPD is (1/2)(OA + PD)·AD = (1/2)(2 + 4)(4sqrt(2)) = 12sqrt(2). The lower trapezoid OBCP is congruent to it, and its area is also 12sqrt(2). Therefore the area of hexagon AOBCPD is 2·12sqrt(2) = 24sqrt(2).

method.method_draft: Partition the hexagon along segment OP into two congruent trapezoids, AOPD and OBCP. From the text, the radii are OA=OB=2 and PC=PD=4, and the centers are externally tangent, so OP=2+4=6. From the image, AD and BC are the upper and lower common external tangents, so OA and PD are both perpendicular to AD, and OB and PC are both perpendicular to BC. For one tangent, use the standard external-tangent right triangle: the separation of centers OP=6 is the hypotenuse, the difference of radii is 4-2=2, so the tangent segment length is AD=BC=sqrt(6^2-2^2)=4sqrt(2). Each half, such as trapezoid AOPD, has parallel bases OA=2 and PD=4 and height AD=4sqrt(2), so its area is (1/2)(2+4)(4sqrt(2))=12sqrt(2). Double for the two congruent trapezoids to get 24sqrt(2).

Let the upper common external tangent have equation y=mx+b. Its distance from O must be 2 and its distance from P must be 4, giving b/sqrt(1+m^2)=2 and (6m+b)/sqrt(1+m^2)=4. Hence m/sqrt(1+m^2)=1/3, so m=1/(2sqrt(2)) and b=3/sqrt(2). Find the tangent points as feet of perpendiculars from the centers to this line: A=(-2/3,4sqrt(2)/3) and D=(14/3,8sqrt(2)/3). By symmetry, B=(-2/3,-4sqrt(2)/3) and C=(14/3,-8sqrt(2)/3). Use the vertex order A,O,B,C,P,D in the shoelace formula; substituting these coordinates gives area 24sqrt(2).
